summary: Explains problems with the DIGEST-MD5 SASL authentication mechanism from RFC 2831, marks it obsolete in the IANA SASL registry, and moves RFC 2831 to Historic status.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC explains why DIGEST-MD5 was withdrawn. The mechanism lets a client prove its identity with a user name and password over any protocol with a SASL profile, but the rules were ambiguous, the syntax was confusing, and the cryptography was outdated. The document lists the faults, marks the mechanism as obsolete in the IANA registry, and points to SCRAM as the replacement.

questions: why was digest-md5 moved to historic
subtitle: The case against DIGEST-MD5, the SASL mechanism that this document moves to Historic.

tldr.problem: DIGEST-MD5, a SASL mechanism for proving who you are with a user name and password, was specified in 2000 and proved hard to implement correctly, ambiguous in places and weak in others.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lists the problems with the mechanism one by one: too many options, confusing syntax, unclear realm handling, an unusable inner hash, inadequate security layers, no protection against interception, missing features and outdated cryptography.
tldr.outcome: It marks DIGEST-MD5 as OBSOLETE in the IANA SASL mechanism registry and moves RFC 2831 to Historic status, pointing at the SCRAM family of mechanisms as the way forward.

facts.label: Inner hash
facts.value: An MD5 hash of the colon-separated user name, realm and password

facts.label: Intended use
facts.value: Any protocol that has a SASL profile, as an improvement on CRAM-MD5

facts.label: Registry status
facts.value: The intended usage of DIGEST-MD5 in the SASL mechanism registry is now OBSOLETE

facts.label: Successor named
facts.value: The SCRAM family of SASL mechanisms

facts.label: Character handling
facts.value: User names and passwords that fit ISO-8859-1 must be converted down from UTF-8

facts.label: Strongest criticism
facts.value: The MD5 hash is weak enough to make a brute force attack easy with common hardware

today: RFC 6331 was published in July 2011 as an Informational document. It marks DIGEST-MD5 as OBSOLETE in the IANA SASL mechanism registry and moves RFC 2831 to Historic status. It has not been obsoleted or updated since.

sections.title: Why DIGEST-MD5 Was Retired
sections.content:
RFC 2831 defines how HTTP Digest Authentication can be used as a Simple Authentication and Security Layer mechanism for any protocol that has a SASL profile. It was intended both as an improvement over CRAM-MD5 and as a convenient way to support a single authentication mechanism for web, email, the Lightweight Directory Access Protocol and other protocols.

It can be argued that it is an improvement over CRAM-MD5, but many implementors commented that the additional complexity of DIGEST-MD5 makes it difficult to implement fully and securely. The RFC then lists an incomplete set of problems with the mechanism as specified.

Because DIGEST-MD5 is defined as an extensible mechanism, it would be possible to fix most of the problems. The RFC argues that doing so would increase the implementation complexity of an already complex mechanism even further, so the effort is not worth the cost. It adds that an implementation of a fixed DIGEST-MD5 specification would likely either fail to interoperate with any existing implementation of RFC 2831, or would be vulnerable to various downgrade attacks.

Despite DIGEST-MD5 having seen some deployment on the Internet, the RFC recommends obsoleting it, because as implemented it is not a reasonable candidate for further standardization and should be deprecated in favour of one or more new password-based mechanisms. The Salted Challenge Response Authentication Mechanism family of SASL mechanisms has been developed to provide similar features with a better design.
sections.plainLanguage: The mechanism could have been patched, since it was designed to be extended. The RFC judges that repairing it would make an already complicated protocol even harder to build correctly, and that a fixed version would probably not talk to the versions already in use. So it was retired rather than repaired, and SCRAM was named as the mechanism to use instead.

sections.title: Too Many Options and Confusing Syntax
sections.content:
The first problem listed is that the mechanism has too many options and modes, some of them not well described and not widely implemented. DIGEST-MD5 allows the qop directive to contain multiple values, but it also allows multiple qop directives to be specified, and the handling of multiple options is not specified. The result is minor interoperability problems: some implementations amalgamate multiple qop values into one, while others treat multiple qop values as an error. Another example is an empty authorization identity. In SASL, an empty authorization identity means that the client is willing to authorize as the authentication identity, but the document is not clear on whether the field must be omitted or can be given with an empty value to convey this. The requirement for backward compatibility with HTTP Digest makes the situation worse. For example, DIGEST-MD5 requires all user names and passwords that can be entirely represented in the ISO-8859-1 charset to be converted down from UTF-8. The use of quoted strings is another example: handling of characters that need escaping is not properly described, and the document has no examples to demonstrate correct behaviour.

The second problem is the syntax. The DIGEST-MD5 document uses ABNF from RFC 822, which allows an extra construct and allows implied folding whitespace to be inserted in many places. The difference from the more common ABNF defined in RFC 5234 is confusing for some implementors, and as a result many implementations do not accept folding whitespace in many of the places where it is allowed.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules left room for two different readings, so different implementations behaved differently and stopped talking to each other. The grammar used was also an older one that allows spaces to be folded across lines, which many implementations did not accept even though the document allowed it.

sections.title: Realms, Stored Hashes and Security Layers
sections.content:
The third problem is the realm. The mechanism uses a realm to define a collection of accounts, and a server can support one or more of them, but the document gives no guidance on how realms should be named, or, more importantly, how they can be entered in user interfaces. As a result, many clients have confusing user interfaces, do not allow users to enter a realm, and or do not let users pick one of the realms the server supports.

The fourth problem is the use of the user name in the inner hash. The inner hash of DIGEST-MD5 is an MD5 hash of the colon-separated user name, realm and password. Implementations may choose to store inner hashes instead of clear text passwords, which has some useful properties, such as protection from a compromise of authentication databases that hold the same user name and password on other servers. This is rarely done in practice, because the inner hash is not compatible with widely deployed Unix password databases, and because changing the user name would invalidate the inner hash.

The fifth problem is that the descriptions of the DES and 3DES and RC4 security layers are inadequate to produce independently developed interoperable implementations. In the DES and 3DES case this is partly a problem with existing DES APIs.
sections.plainLanguage: The account area, called a realm, had no naming rules and no way for a user to pick one, so client programs ended up with confusing prompts. Storing a hashed password instead of the password itself was possible but fitted badly with the password files that Unix systems already had, and it broke as soon as a user changed their user name. The optional encryption layers were described too loosely for two independent teams to build compatible software.

sections.title: Attack Surface and Missing Features
sections.content:
The sixth problem is that the outer hash, the value of the response directive, does not protect the whole authentication exchange. That makes the mechanism vulnerable to man-in-the-middle attacks, such as modification of the list of supported qop values or ciphers.

The seventh problem is a list of features that are missing, which makes the mechanism insecure or unsuitable for use in protocols. There are no channel bindings. There is no hash agility, meaning no easy way to replace the MD5 hash function with another one. And there is no support for SASLPrep or any other kind of Unicode character normalization of user names and passwords: the original document predates SASLPrep and recommends no normalization at all.

The eighth problem is that the cryptographic primitives are not up to today's standards. The MD5 hash is sufficiently weak to make a brute force attack on DIGEST-MD5 easy with common hardware. The RC4 algorithm is prone to attack when used as the security layer without discarding the initial key stream output. And the DES cipher for the security layer is considered insecure because of its small key space. The RFC notes that most of these problems are already present in the HTTP Digest authentication mechanism. Its Security Considerations section adds only one sentence: security issues are discussed throughout the document.
sections.plainLanguage: Someone in the middle could change the list of offered options and the exchange would still go through, because only part of it was protected. The mechanism also lacked features that later protocols expect, such as tying the login to the encrypted channel it runs over. And the underlying cryptography, MD5, RC4 and DES, had all fallen below an acceptable standard.

sections.title: The IANA Registry Change
sections.content:
IANA changed the intended usage of the DIGEST-MD5 mechanism registration in the SASL mechanism registry to OBSOLETE. The SASL mechanism registry is specified by RFC 4422.

The change is administrative rather than technical: the mechanism itself is untouched, and this document does not describe any protocol behaviour. What it does is record that the mechanism is no longer one that anyone should build into new software, and that the document which defined it, RFC 2831, has moved to Historic status.
sections.plainLanguage: The practical effect is a line in a central registry that says do not use this mechanism in new software. Nothing about the protocol itself changed; what changed is the official record of whether it is worth building.

viz.caption: THE FAULTS THE RFC LISTS WITH DIGEST-MD5

items.title: Too many options
items.text: Too many options and modes, some of them not well described and not widely implemented, which causes minor interoperability problems.

items.title: Confusing grammar
items.text: The ABNF of RFC 822 is used, with its extra construct and implied folding whitespace, and many implementations do not accept the whitespace the document allows.

items.title: Realm handling
items.text: No guidance on naming realms or letting a user pick one in a user interface, so many clients have confusing interfaces.

items.title: User name in the inner hash
items.text: The stored inner hash is not compatible with widely deployed Unix password databases, and changing the user name invalidates it.

items.title: Weak security layers
items.text: The DES, 3DES and RC4 descriptions are inadequate to produce independently developed interoperable implementations.

items.title: Missing features
items.text: No channel bindings, no hash agility and no Unicode normalization of user names and passwords.

items.title: Unprotected exchange
items.text: The outer hash does not protect the whole exchange, so the mechanism is vulnerable to man-in-the-middle attacks.

items.title: Outdated cryptography
items.text: MD5 is weak enough for an easy brute force attack, and RC4 and DES are both considered insecure.
